quiz_cs101_f23_midterm.title: Fall 2023 Midterm Examination — Introduction to Algorithms (Past Year)
quiz_cs101_f23_midterm.description: Past year midterm exam with 15 problems covering asymptotic analysis, sorting, graphs, hashing, and complexity theory. Based on MIT 6.006. To be used as template for Fall 2024 midterm revision.

questions.text: True or False: 2^(2n) is in Theta(2^n). Justify your answer.

choices.C: believing constant factors in exponents don't matter

questions.solution: False. 2^(2n) = (2^n)^2. This is equivalent to asking whether k^2 is in Theta(k) for k=2^n, which is false. Constants in exponents matter asymptotically.

questions.text: True or False: Performing an O(1) amortized operation n times on an initially empty data structure takes worst-case O(n) time. Justify.

choices.C: thinking worst-case per-operation must be O(1)

questions.solution: True. This is the definition of amortized analysis: if each operation costs O(1) amortized, then n operations on an initially empty structure cost at most O(n) total worst-case time.

questions.text: True or False: Given an array A of n items, when sorting A via merge sort, each item is compared with O(log n) other items. Justify.

choices.B: confusing tree depth O(log n) with per-item comparisons
choices.C: only counting one level of recursion

questions.solution: False. During the final merge of two sorted halves of size Theta(n), a single item from one half may be compared with all items from the other half. So an item can participate in Theta(n) comparisons, not O(log n).

questions.text: True or False: Given a binary min-heap of n items with comparable keys, one can build a Set AVL Tree containing the same items using O(n) comparisons. Justify.

choices.B: not recognizing the reduction to sorting
choices.C: believing heap already provides sorted order

questions.solution: False. If such an algorithm existed, we could sort n items in O(n) time: build a min-heap in O(n), convert to AVL in O(n), then read in-order in O(n). This contradicts the Omega(n log n) comparison sort lower bound.

questions.text: True or False: Given a directed graph G=(V,E), run BFS from vertex s. While processing vertex u, if some v in Adj(u) has already been processed, then G contains a directed cycle. Justify.

choices.B: assuming BFS cross-edges imply cycles in directed graphs
choices.C: confusing directed and undirected cycle detection

questions.solution: False. BFS cannot detect directed cycles this way. Counterexample: V={s,a,b,t}, E={(s,t),(s,a),(a,b),(b,t)}. BFS from s processes levels {s}, {a,t}, {b}. When processing b, vertex t in Adj(b) was already processed, yet G is a DAG (no cycle).

questions.text: True or False: Run Bellman-Ford on weighted graph G=(V,E,w) from vertex s. If there is a witness v (i.e., delta_|V|(s,v) < delta_{|V|-1}(s,v)), then v is on a negative-weight cycle. Justify.
questions.solution: False. A witness vertex v is only guaranteed to be REACHABLE from a negative-weight cycle; it may not actually be ON the cycle itself. The relaxation propagates improvements beyond the cycle.

questions.text: True or False: Floyd-Warshall and Johnson's Algorithm solve all-pairs shortest paths in the same asymptotic running time when applied to complete graphs (|E| = Theta(|V|^2)). Justify.
questions.solution: True. Floyd-Warshall runs in O(|V|^3). For complete graphs, |E|=Theta(|V|^2), so Johnson's runs in O(|V|^2 log|V| + |V||E|) = O(|V|^3). Same asymptotic time.

questions.text: True or False: If there is a polynomial-time algorithm for 0-1 Knapsack, then there is also a polynomial-time algorithm for Subset Sum. Justify.

choices.B: confusing which problem reduces to which
choices.C: not seeing Subset Sum as a special case

questions.solution: True. Subset Sum is a special case of 0-1 Knapsack: convert instance (A,T) by setting item i to have size=a_i and value=a_i, with knapsack capacity T. If knapsack achieves value T, subset summing to T exists. Linear-time reduction.

questions.text: An integer array A is k-even-mixed: exactly k=ceil(n/lg n) even integers, and odd integers appear in sorted order. Describe an O(n)-time algorithm to sort A.

choices.A: Separate evens/odds, sort evens in O(k log k)=O(n), merge in O(n)
choices.B: using insertion sort for evens (O(k^2) not O(n))
choices.C: trying radix/counting sort instead of comparison sort

questions.solution: Scan A, separate evens into AE and odds into AO. AO is already sorted (given). Sort AE via merge sort in O(k log k) = O((n/lg n) * log(n/lg n)) = O(n). Merge sorted AE and AO in O(n). Total: O(n).

questions.text: Given n pairs of positive integers (x_i, y_i) with x_i, y_i < n^2, the power of (x,y) is x + n*y. Describe an O(n)-time algorithm to sort pairs by power.

choices.A: Separate y=1 case, radix sort each group, merge in O(n)

questions.solution: Handle y=1 separately (power=x+n, bounded by O(n^2), radix sort in O(n)). For y>1, use tuple sort: stable radix sort by x, then by y. Values bounded by O(n^2), so radix sort is O(n) per pass. Merge the two sorted arrays in O(n). Total O(n).

questions.text: Given an array A of n distinct positive integers, describe an O(n^2)-time algorithm to determine whether four integers from A form a Pythagorean Quad (a,b,c,d) where d = sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2). Integers may repeat.

choices.A: Hash all a^2+b^2 values, then lookup d^2-c^2 for each pair

questions.solution: Observe: a^2+b^2 = d^2-c^2. Build hash table H of all a^2+b^2 for O(n^2) pairs. For each (c,d) pair, lookup d^2-c^2 in H. If found, quad exists. O(n^2) expected time.

questions.text: Given a connected undirected weighted graph G=(V,E,w) with unique edge weights, describe an O(|E| log |E|)-time algorithm to find the largest k such that removing all edges with weight >= k disconnects the graph.

choices.A: Sort edges, binary search on threshold k, check connectivity at each step
choices.B: linearly scanning all thresholds instead of binary search

questions.solution: Sort edge weights in O(|E| log |E|). Binary search on k: for candidate k', run BFS/DFS on edges with weight < k' to check connectivity in O(|E|). O(log |E|) binary search steps, each O(|E|). Total: O(|E| log |E|).

questions.text: Friends want to drive from city A to city B in at most d days, spending at most b on expenses. Each city c_i has hotel cost h(c_i) and at most 10 neighboring cities with driving costs. Describe an O(nd)-time algorithm to determine feasibility.

choices.A: Time-expanded DAG with (city,day) vertices, DAG relaxation
choices.B: not including hotel costs in edge weights
choices.C: only checking d-day paths (missing shorter trips)

questions.solution: Build graph with vertex (city, day) for each city and day 0..d. Edge ((c_i,d'),(c_j,d'+1)) with weight g(c_i,c_j)+h(c_j). Graph is DAG (day always increases). Run DAG relaxation from (A,0). Check if delta((A,0),(B,d')) <= b for any d'. O(nd) vertices and O(nd) edges (degree <= 10).

questions.text: True or False: If a decision problem A has a pseudopolynomial-time algorithm, and P != NP, then A is not solvable in polynomial time. Justify.
questions.solution: False. A problem can have both a pseudopolynomial-time algorithm AND a polynomial-time algorithm. In fact, every polynomial-time algorithm is also pseudopolynomial-time. Having a pseudopolynomial algorithm doesn't prevent having a polynomial one.

questions.text: Design a database for a wildlife park. Support: initialize() in O(1), add_sighting(species,zone) in O(log n), remove_oldest() in O(log n), is_common(species) in O(1) where common means >= 100 sightings in any single zone. Describe your data structures.

choices.A: Hash table + augmented AVL trees + linked list for ordering
choices.C: not maintaining insertion order for remove_oldest

questions.solution: Hash table H mapping species to augmented Set AVL tree T_s. Each T_s stores (zone, count) pairs keyed by zone, augmented with max count in subtree. Doubly-linked list L for insertion order. add_sighting: lookup/update T_s and append to L. remove_oldest: pop front of L, decrement count in T_s. is_common: check root max >= 100 in O(1).

questions.text: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Starting with 3 mol H₂ and 2 mol O₂, which is the limiting reagent?

In the reaction 2Fe³⁺ + Sn²⁺ → 2Fe²⁺ + Sn⁴⁺, identify the reducing agent.

questions.text: A farmer can produce 100 kg wheat OR 50 kg corn. The opportunity cost of 1 kg corn is:
questions.solution: OC of 1 corn = 100/50 = 2 wheat

questions.text: Country A: 10 cars or 30 computers/day. Country B: 6 cars or 24 computers/day. Who has comparative advantage in cars?

choices.A: Country A (OC = 3 computers per car vs B's 4)

questions.solution: A: OC(car) = 30/10 = 3 computers. B: OC(car) = 24/6 = 4 computers. A has lower OC for cars.

questions.text: If countries specialize according to comparative advantage and trade, total world output:
questions.solution: Specialization per comparative advantage maximizes total output.

questions.text: A country operates inside its PPF. This means:
questions.solution: Points inside PPF indicate unused resources or inefficiency.

questions.text: Qd = 100 - 2P, Qs = 20 + 3P. Find the equilibrium price.
Price rises from $10 to $12, quantity demanded falls from 100 to 80. Calculate PED (midpoint method).
Demand curve: P = 50 - Q. Equilibrium at P=20, Q=30. Find consumer surplus.
questions.solution: CS = ½ × base × height = ½ × 30 × (50-20) = $450

questions.text: A factory pollutes a river. Without government intervention, the market produces:

choices.A: More than the socially optimal quantity
choices.B: Less than the socially optimal quantity

questions.solution: Negative externality → social cost > private cost → overproduction

questions.text: A monopolist faces P = 100 - 2Q, TC = 20Q. Find profit-maximizing quantity.
In long-run equilibrium for a perfectly competitive firm:
questions.solution: Free entry/exit drives economic profit to zero: P = MC = min ATC

questions.text: Which is NOT included in GDP? (a) haircuts, (b) used car sales, (c) new car production.
questions.solution: Used goods were counted in GDP when first produced.

questions.text: A per-unit tax is placed on sellers. The tax burden falls more on consumers when:
questions.solution: More inelastic side bears more of the tax burden.

questions.text: National defense is a public good because it is:
questions.solution: Public goods: non-rival (one person's consumption doesn't reduce availability) and non-excludable.

questions.text: A firm hires workers: 1→10 units, 2→25, 3→35, 4→42. Marginal product of the 4th worker is:
questions.solution: MP₄ = 42 - 35 = 7 units

questions.text: In a Prisoner's Dilemma, the dominant strategy for each player is:
questions.solution: Defecting is strictly dominant: better payoff regardless of other player's choice.

X takes values {1,2,3,4} with P(X=k) = k/10. Is this a valid PMF?
questions.solution: Sum = (1+2+3+4)/10 = 10/10 = 1.0. All non-negative. Valid PMF.

A p-value of 0.03 means:

choices.A: If H₀ true, probability of seeing data this extreme or more is 3%
choices.B: There is a 3% probability H₀ is true

questions.solution: P-value = P(data ≥ observed | H₀ true). NOT P(H₀ true).

questions.text: Sample mean=100, SE=5, z*=1.96 for 95% CI. Find the interval.
A Type II error occurs when:

choices.A: Failing to reject H₀ when H₁ is true
choices.B: Rejecting H₀ when H₀ is true
choices.C: Rejecting H₁ when H₁ is true

questions.solution: Type I: reject true H₀ (α). Type II: fail to reject false H₀ (β).

questions.text: Ice cream sales and drownings are positively correlated. This proves:
questions.solution: Correlation ≠ causation. Temperature is a confounding variable.

questions.text: Regression: y = 2.5x + 10. For each unit increase in x, y increases by:
questions.solution: Slope = 2.5 means Δy/Δx = 2.5

questions.text: A χ² test for independence has df=4 and test statistic=11.5. Critical value at α=0.05 is 9.49. Conclusion?

choices.B: Fail to reject (compare to wrong table)

questions.solution: 11.5 > 9.49 → reject H₀ at α=0.05. Evidence of association.

quiz_ml201_f23_midterm.title: Fall 2023 Midterm Examination — Machine Learning (Past Year)
quiz_ml201_f23_midterm.description: Past year midterm exam with 15 problems covering supervised/unsupervised learning, neural networks, and model evaluation.

questions.text: Train accuracy=99%, test accuracy=55%. What is the most likely issue?
questions.solution: Large train-test gap indicates overfitting.

questions.text: A linear model on highly nonlinear data shows high training error. This indicates:
questions.solution: High train error = model too simple = high bias.

questions.text: L2 regularization (ridge) primarily reduces model complexity by:
questions.solution: L2 penalty ||w||² shrinks weights but doesn't zero them (unlike L1).

questions.text: Why hold out a separate test set?

choices.A: To estimate generalization error on unseen data

questions.solution: Test set = final unbiased estimate of out-of-sample performance.

questions.text: In gradient descent, the learning rate α is too large. What happens?
questions.solution: Too-large α overshoots minima → divergence.

questions.text: A decision tree chooses the feature split that maximizes:
questions.solution: Greedy: pick feature+threshold maximizing IG (entropy) or Gini reduction.

questions.text: In KNN classification, increasing k from 1 to 100 in a noisy dataset generally:
questions.solution: Larger k = smoother boundary = less variance, more bias.

questions.text: In a linear SVM, the margin is defined as:

choices.A: 2/||w|| (distance between decision boundary and nearest support vectors)

questions.solution: Margin = 2/||w||. SVM maximizes this by minimizing ||w||².

questions.text: 5-fold cross-validation splits data into 5 parts and:

choices.A: Trains on 4 parts, validates on 1 part, rotates 5 times
choices.C: Uses 1 part for training, 4 for validation

questions.solution: Each fold: 80% train, 20% val. Average 5 results.

questions.text: In a medical diagnosis model, if we increase the classification threshold, precision typically:
questions.solution: Higher threshold → fewer positives → higher precision, lower recall.

questions.text: Backpropagation computes gradients using:

choices.A: Chain rule of calculus applied layer by layer

questions.solution: Backprop = reverse-mode auto-differentiation using chain rule.

questions.text: PCA finds directions of maximum variance. The first principal component captures:

choices.A: The direction of greatest variance in the data

questions.solution: PC1 = eigenvector with largest eigenvalue = max variance direction.

questions.text: K-means clustering with K=3 converges when:

choices.A: Cluster assignments stop changing between iterations
choices.C: All points are in the same cluster

questions.solution: Convergence = no reassignment. Guaranteed to converge (local optimum).

questions.text: Random forests reduce overfitting compared to a single decision tree by:

choices.A: Training many trees on bootstrap samples and averaging predictions

questions.solution: Bagging + feature randomization → decorrelated trees → variance reduction.

questions.text: Why is feature scaling important for gradient descent-based algorithms?

choices.A: Features on different scales cause elongated cost surface → slow convergence
choices.B: It increases the number of features

questions.solution: Unscaled features → different gradient magnitudes → zigzag path → slow convergence.

slides.title: Hypothesis Testing — Week 7 Overview
slides.body:
Topics:
• Null and alternative hypotheses
• Type I and Type II errors
• The p-value (traditional interpretation: p < 0.05 is 'significant')
• One-sample z-test and t-test
slides.speaker_notes: Remind students that all examples this week use NHST (Null Hypothesis Significance Testing), the dominant framework since Fisher (1935).

slides.title: The p-value Debate (pre-2019 view)
slides.body:
• p-value: probability of data at least as extreme as observed, given H0 is true
• Threshold α = 0.05 widely accepted since Fisher (1925)
• Binary decision: reject H0 if p < 0.05, fail to reject otherwise
• Criticism: p-hacking, file-drawer problem (Simmons et al. 2011)
• Solution proposed: pre-registration of studies
slides.speaker_notes: Note: This slide presents the state of the debate as of 2018. The field has moved significantly since then — see the 2019 Nature commentary and 2021 American Statistician special issue.

slides.title: Effect Size and Power
slides.body:
• Cohen's d: standardised effect size (small=0.2, medium=0.5, large=0.8)
• Statistical power = 1 − β (probability of detecting a true effect)
• Rule of thumb: aim for 80% power (Cohen, 1988)
• G*Power software for sample size calculation
• Limitation: power analysis often done post-hoc (questionable practice)
slides.speaker_notes: G*Power version shown here is 3.0 (2007). Students should download current version 3.1.

slides.title: Bayesian Alternatives (brief mention)
slides.body:
• Bayesian inference uses prior + likelihood → posterior
• Bayes Factor (BF): ratio of evidence for H1 vs H0
• BF > 3: moderate evidence for H1 (Jeffreys, 1961)
• Not widely adopted in social sciences as of 2018
• Software: JASP (2016, free)
slides.speaker_notes: Bayesian methods were niche in 2018 but adoption is growing. Updated content should reflect the current landscape in 2024.

slides.title: Replication Crisis — Where We Stood in 2015
slides.body:
• OSC (2015): only 36–39% of psychology findings replicated
• Many issues: small samples, p-hacking, HARKing
• Solution: Open Science practices, pre-registration
• APA Task Force on Statistical Inference (1999) recommendations largely ignored
slides.speaker_notes: This slide needs a major update: the replication crisis landscape has evolved substantially since 2015. See Nosek et al. (2022) and recent meta-science work.

slides.title: Review: Conditional Probability (Foundation)
slides.body:
• Conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(A∩B) / P(B)
• Law of Total Probability: P(A) = Σ P(A|Bᵢ)·P(Bᵢ)
• Key example: P(disease|positive test) vs P(positive test|disease)
NOTE: This foundation underpins Bayesian inference covered above.
⚠ Midterm data shows this area needs reinforcement — see quiz_stat20_mid results.

prs_cs101_w9_ml_intro.title: CS101 Week 9 — Introduction to Machine Learning

slides.title: Machine Learning — Week 9 Overview
slides.body:
Topics:
• Supervised vs unsupervised learning
• Classic algorithms: linear regression, decision trees, SVM
• Deep learning basics (2019 perspective)
• Popular frameworks: TensorFlow 1.x, Keras, scikit-learn 0.21
slides.speaker_notes: This deck was last updated in early 2020. The ML landscape has changed dramatically — LLMs, diffusion models, and new frameworks (PyTorch dominance, HuggingFace) deserve coverage.

slides.title: The Deep Learning Revolution (2012–2019)
slides.body:
• AlexNet (2012): CNN breakthrough on ImageNet
• GAN (Goodfellow 2014): generative adversarial networks
• Transformer (Vaswani 2017): attention is all you need
• BERT (2018), GPT-2 (2019): large language models emerge
• Current SOTA: GPT-2 with 1.5B parameters
slides.speaker_notes: GPT-2 is now considered small. Students should understand the scale jump: GPT-3 (175B, 2020) → ChatGPT/GPT-4 era. This slide needs updating to reflect 2022–2024 developments.

slides.title: Training Data and Datasets
slides.body:
• ImageNet: 14M images, 1000 classes (the standard benchmark since 2010)
• Common Crawl: web-scale text for NLP
• Benchmark: GLUE (2018) for NLP tasks
• Data collection: manual labelling via Mechanical Turk
• Limitation: bias in training data not well understood
slides.speaker_notes: GLUE has been superseded by SuperGLUE then BIG-Bench. The data quality/synthetic data debate is now central to ML research.

slides.title: AI Ethics and Fairness (2019 view)
slides.body:
• Algorithmic bias: facial recognition errors on darker skin (Buolamwini & Gebru 2018)
• Fairness definitions: demographic parity, equalised odds
• Explainability: LIME (2016), SHAP (2017)
• EU GDPR (2018): 'right to explanation'
• Calls for AI regulation — largely unaddressed as of 2019
slides.speaker_notes: EU AI Act was passed in 2024. This slide needs significant update: EU AI Act, US EO on AI Safety, model cards, responsible scaling policies.

slides.title: Hands-On Tools for Students
slides.body:
• Scikit-learn: go-to for classical ML
• Keras/TensorFlow 1.x: deep learning
• Google Colab: free GPU access (T4 GPUs)
• Kaggle competitions: learn by doing
• Recommended reading: Géron (2019) 'Hands-On ML'
slides.speaker_notes: PyTorch has overtaken TensorFlow among researchers. HuggingFace Transformers is now essential. Recommend updating to Géron (2022, 3rd ed.) and adding HuggingFace tutorial.

slides.title: Advanced Integration — Week 12 Overview
slides.body:
Topics: u-substitution, trigonometric integration, improper integrals, convergence tests
KC coverage: integration_by_substitution, trig_identities_for_integration, integral_of_sec_and_sec_squared, improper_integral_interior_singularity, limit_definition_of_improper_integral, divergence_detection

slides.title: Integration by Substitution (u-substitution)
slides.body:
Substitution rule: ∫f(g(x))g'(x)dx = ∫f(u)du
Standard patterns: ∫2x·(x²+1)⁵dx, ∫e^(x²)·2x dx
Note: this slide covers only polynomial and exponential composites; trig substitutions handled on slide_02

slides.title: Trigonometric Integration (2018 curriculum — incomplete)
slides.body:
Key identities: sin²x + cos²x = 1, 1 + tan²x = sec²x
∫sec²x dx = tan x + C
∫sec x tan x dx = sec x + C
NOTE: This slide uses the 2018 formula sheet only — the half-angle identity approach and ∫sec³x dx worked example are missing. Students consistently report confusion on sec³x problems.
slides.speaker_notes: Update needed: add sec³x worked example using integration by parts + half-angle identity approach

slides.title: Improper Integrals — Type I only (gap: Type II missing)
slides.body:
Type I (infinite limits): ∫₁^∞ 1/x² dx = lim_{b→∞} ∫₁^b 1/x² dx = 1
p-series test: ∫₁^∞ 1/xᵖ dx converges iff p > 1
NOTE: Type II improper integrals (interior singularity, e.g., ∫₀¹ 1/√x dx) are NOT covered — this was removed in the 2019 revision and is a known gap. Exam questions on interior singularities are frequently missed.
slides.speaker_notes: CRITICAL: Add Type II (interior singularity) with worked example ∫₀¹ 1/√x dx

slides.title: Divergence Detection and Comparison Tests
slides.body:
Direct Comparison: 0 ≤ f(x) ≤ g(x) and ∫g converges → ∫f converges
Limit Comparison: lim_{x→∞} f(x)/g(x) = L > 0 → same convergence behavior
Divergence example: ∫₁^∞ 1/x dx diverges (harmonic series)
Note: p-series and alternating series tests not included here

slides.title: Overfitting & Regularisation — Week 5 Overview
slides.body:
Topics: overfitting diagnosis, bias-variance tradeoff, L1/L2 regularisation, cross-validation
KC coverage: overfitting_definition_and_diagnosis, bias_variance_tradeoff_formal, regularization_as_variance_reduction, cross_validation_concept, model_complexity_and_generalization

slides.title: Overfitting and the Bias-Variance Tradeoff (classical view only)
slides.body:
Overfitting: model memorises training data, high variance, poor generalisation
Bias-Variance decomposition: E[L] = Bias² + Variance + Noise
Classical U-curve: complexity↑ → variance↑ monotonically
NOTE: Double descent phenomenon (Belkin et al., 2019) — where test error decreases again at very high model complexity after an initial peak — is NOT covered here. This is a significant gap for a 2024 ML curriculum.
slides.speaker_notes: Update: add double descent curve, interpolation threshold, and modern NTK theory reference

slides.title: Regularisation as Variance Reduction
slides.body:
L2 (Ridge): loss += λ‖w‖₂² — shrinks weights toward zero, no sparsity
L1 (Lasso): loss += λ‖w‖₁ — induces feature sparsity, automatic selection
Elastic Net: α·L1 + (1-α)·L2 — combines both
Effect: regularisation trades variance reduction for bias increase; optimal λ via CV

slides.title: Cross-Validation for Model Selection
slides.body:
k-fold CV: partition data into k folds, train on k-1 folds, evaluate on held-out fold, rotate
Common choices: k=5 or k=10
Nested CV: inner loop selects hyperparameters, outer loop estimates generalisation error
Note: time-series CV and group-stratified CV variants not covered

slides.title: Model Complexity Management (2019 guidelines — outdated)
slides.body:
Practical guidelines (2019 vintage):
1. Start simple, add complexity only when validation loss improves
2. Use held-out validation set throughout training
3. Report test metrics only once at the end
NOTE: This slide pre-dates modern best practices: early stopping with patience, learning curve analysis, AutoML tools (Optuna, Ray Tune), and foundation model fine-tuning are not mentioned.
slides.speaker_notes: Update: add early stopping, learning curves, and mention modern AutoML approaches

slides.title: Multiple Linear Regression — Week 10 Overview
slides.body:
Topics: OLS geometry, multicollinearity, VIF, model selection, ridge regression
KC coverage: ordinary_least_squares_geometry, multicollinearity_definition_and_effect, variance_inflation_factor_intuition, model_selection_and_parsimony, ridge_regression_as_fix

slides.title: OLS Estimation — Algebraic Derivation (no geometric intuition)
slides.body:
β̂ = (X'X)⁻¹X'y — minimises ‖y − Xβ‖²
Four Gauss-Markov assumptions: linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, normality
NOTE: This slide presents only the matrix algebra derivation. The geometric interpretation of OLS (projection of y onto the column space of X) is absent. Research shows students retain the concept better with geometric intuition alongside algebra.
slides.speaker_notes: Consider adding: projection diagram showing ŷ = Hx as orthogonal projection

slides.title: Multicollinearity and Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)
slides.body:
Multicollinearity: correlated predictors X₁, X₂ → inflated standard errors, unstable β̂
VIF_j = 1/(1 − R²_j) where R²_j = R² from regressing Xⱼ on all other predictors
Diagnosis: VIF > 10 = severe; VIF > 5 = moderate concern
Consequence: coefficients become unreliable; individual p-values misleading

slides.title: Model Selection — Stepwise Approach (deprecated method)
slides.body:
Forward stepwise: add predictors sequentially by F-test p-value significance
Backward stepwise: remove predictors with highest p-value iteratively
NOTE: Stepwise selection by p-value is widely criticised (Harrell 2001, APA Statistical Guidelines 2023) for inflating Type I error, overfitting, and non-reproducibility. Modern preferred methods — AIC, BIC, Lasso regularisation, cross-validated model selection — are NOT presented here.
slides.speaker_notes: IMPORTANT: Replace with AIC/BIC guidance and Lasso-based variable selection

slides.title: Ridge Regression as a Fix for Multicollinearity
slides.body:
Ridge estimator: β̂_ridge = (X'X + λI)⁻¹X'y
Key property: adding λ to diagonal ensures (X'X + λI) is always invertible, even with multicollinearity
Bias-variance trade-off: ridge introduces bias but substantially reduces variance
λ selection: cross-validation grid search over λ ∈ {0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10}

prs_phys101_w6_newtons_laws.title: PHYS101 Week 6 — Newton's First and Second Laws

slides.title: Newton's Laws of Motion — Week 6 Overview
slides.body:
Topics:
• Newton's First Law (inertia) and frames of reference
• Newton's Second Law: F = ma (net force and acceleration)
• Free-body diagrams for single objects
• Weight vs mass: W = mg
KC coverage: newton_second_law_basic, vector_decomposition
slides.speaker_notes: Emphasise that F = ma is a vector equation. Students often forget to decompose forces into components before applying it.

slides.title: Newton's First Law — Inertia and Reference Frames
slides.body:
• An object at rest stays at rest; an object in motion stays in motion (unless acted on by net external force)
• Inertial reference frames: frames where Newton's 1st law holds
• Non-inertial frame example: accelerating elevator
• Common misconception: 'force is needed to maintain motion' (Aristotelian view)
slides.speaker_notes: Use the tablecloth-and-dishes demo to illustrate inertia. Ask: 'Why does the dish stay put?'

slides.title: Newton's Second Law — F = ma
slides.body:
• ΣF = ma (net force = mass × acceleration)
• This is a VECTOR equation: must resolve into x and y components
• Units: force in Newtons (N = kg·m/s²)
• Example: 5 kg block, applied force 20 N horizontally
  a = F/m = 20/5 = 4 m/s²
• With friction: a = (F - f)/m
slides.speaker_notes: Stress that students must draw FBD before writing F = ma. Many errors come from forgetting normal force or friction.

slides.title: Free-Body Diagrams and Force Decomposition
slides.body:
• Step 1: Identify the object (isolate it)
• Step 2: Draw ALL forces acting ON the object
  - Weight (mg, downward)
  - Normal force (perpendicular to surface)
  - Friction (parallel to surface, opposing motion)
  - Applied force (as specified)
• Step 3: Choose coordinate axes (often along incline)
• Step 4: Resolve each force into components
slides.speaker_notes: The inclined plane problem on the next slide is the most common exam question format.

slides.title: Practice Problem — Block on an Incline (no friction)
slides.body:
A 3 kg block slides down a frictionless 30° incline.
• Weight decomposition: mg sinθ (along incline), mg cosθ (perpendicular)
• Normal force N = mg cosθ = 3(9.8)cos30° ≈ 25.5 N
• Acceleration along incline: a = g sinθ = 9.8 sin30° = 4.9 m/s²
Note: acceleration is independent of mass on frictionless incline (like Galileo's result!)
slides.speaker_notes: Ask students to predict: 'If we double the mass, what happens to the acceleration?' Most will incorrectly say it doubles.

prs_bio101_w7_pedigree.title: BIO101 Week 7 — Pedigree Analysis and Inheritance Patterns

slides.title: Pedigree Analysis — Week 7 Midterm Review
slides.body:
Topics:
• Pedigree symbols and conventions
• Autosomal recessive vs dominant patterns
• X-linked recessive vs dominant patterns
• Strategy: elimination approach for inheritance mode
KC coverage: pedigree_pattern_discrimination, autosomal_recessive_carrier_logic
slides.speaker_notes: This is the midterm review week. Focus on the decision tree for pedigree discrimination.

slides.title: Pedigree Symbols and Notation
slides.body:
• Circles = female, squares = male
• Filled = affected, open = unaffected
• Half-filled = carrier (heterozygous for recessive trait)
• Horizontal line = mating, vertical line = offspring
• Roman numerals = generations (I, II, III)
• Arabic numerals = individuals within generation (II-3, II-4)

slides.title: Autosomal Recessive — Key Indicators
slides.body:
• Trait skips generations (carriers are unaffected)
• Affected children can have unaffected parents (both carriers: Aa × Aa)
• Roughly 1/4 of children from carrier × carrier are affected
• Males and females affected equally
• Classic example: cystic fibrosis, sickle cell anemia
• Rule-out test: affected child from two unaffected parents → CANNOT be autosomal dominant
slides.speaker_notes: Emphasise the carrier logic: 'If both parents are unaffected but a child is affected, both parents MUST be carriers.'

slides.title: X-Linked Recessive — Key Indicators
slides.body:
• More males affected than females (males hemizygous: X^a Y)
• Affected males get the allele from carrier MOTHERS
• Affected father × carrier mother can produce affected daughters
• No male-to-male transmission (father gives Y, not X)
• Classic examples: hemophilia A, red-green color blindness
• Rule-out test: affected father → affected son = NOT X-linked recessive
slides.speaker_notes: The 'no father-to-son' rule is the fastest way to eliminate X-linked recessive. Students should check this first.

slides.title: Pedigree Discrimination Strategy — Elimination Approach
slides.body:
Step 1: Can it be autosomal dominant? (affected parent rule)
  → If affected child has NO affected parent → rule out AD
Step 2: Can it be X-linked recessive? (no father→son rule)
  → If affected father has affected son → rule out XLR
Step 3: Remaining options: autosomal recessive or X-linked dominant
  → Check sex ratio of affected individuals
  → AR: equal sex ratio; XLD: more females affected
slides.speaker_notes: Walk through 2-3 practice pedigrees using this elimination approach. This is the highest-yield exam strategy.

slides.title: Ideal Gas Law — Week 6 Overview
slides.body:
Topics:
• PV = nRT derivation from empirical gas laws
• Choosing correct R value (0.0821 L·atm/mol·K vs 8.314 J/mol·K)
• Unit conversions: °C → K, mL → L, mmHg → atm
• Problem types: finding P, V, n, or T
KC coverage: ideal_gas_law, stoichiometry_mole_calculations
slides.speaker_notes: Most student errors are unit conversion. Drill the K = °C + 273.15 conversion early.

slides.title: From Empirical Laws to PV = nRT
slides.body:
• Boyle's Law: PV = k (constant T, n) → P ∝ 1/V
• Charles's Law: V/T = k (constant P, n) → V ∝ T
• Avogadro's Law: V/n = k (constant T, P) → V ∝ n
• Combined: PV = nRT where R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K)
• At STP (0°C, 1 atm): 1 mol ideal gas = 22.4 L

slides.title: Common Problem Types
slides.body:
Type 1: Find missing variable
  Given P, V, n → find T: T = PV/(nR)
  Example: 2.0 mol gas at 1.5 atm in 10.0 L vessel: T = (1.5)(10.0)/((2.0)(0.0821)) = 91.4 K

Type 2: Gas stoichiometry
  Use moles from balanced equation + PV = nRT
  Example: How many liters of O₂ at STP from decomposing 2 mol KClO₃?
slides.speaker_notes: Walk through Type 2 step by step: stoichiometry first (moles), then gas law (volume).

slides.title: Unit Conversion Pitfalls
slides.body:
• Temperature MUST be in Kelvin (K = °C + 273.15)
  Common error: using °C directly in PV = nRT
• Pressure: 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 101.325 kPa
• Volume: 1 L = 1000 mL = 0.001 m³
• R value must match units: L·atm → R = 0.0821; J → R = 8.314
• Tip: write R with units and cancel — mismatched units become obvious

slides.title: Limitations of the Ideal Gas Law
slides.body:
• Assumes: no intermolecular forces, negligible molecular volume
• Breaks down at: high pressure (molecules close together) and low temperature (KE ≈ intermolecular PE)
• Real gas correction: van der Waals equation (Week 8)
  (P + a/V²)(V - b) = nRT
• For this course: ideal gas law is sufficient for all problem sets
slides.speaker_notes: Preview: Week 8 covers when ideal gas approximation fails. For now, all problems assume ideal behaviour.

prs_econ101_w5_supply_demand.title: ECON101 Week 5 — Supply and Demand: Market Equilibrium

slides.title: Supply and Demand — Week 5 Overview
slides.body:
Topics:
• Demand curve: law of demand, determinants, shifts
• Supply curve: law of supply, determinants, shifts
• Market equilibrium: where S meets D
• Surplus and shortage: price adjustment mechanism
KC coverage: supply_demand_equilibrium, price_mechanism
slides.speaker_notes: This is the most important single topic in Econ 101. Every subsequent chapter builds on this framework.

slides.title: The Demand Curve
slides.body:
• Law of Demand: price ↑ → quantity demanded ↓ (ceteris paribus)
• Demand curve slopes downward (P on y-axis, Q on x-axis)
• Movement ALONG the curve: caused by price change
• SHIFT of the curve: caused by income, tastes, expectations, related goods
• Normal good: income ↑ → demand ↑; Inferior good: income ↑ → demand ↓
slides.speaker_notes: Biggest student confusion: movement along vs shift. Drill with examples.

slides.title: The Supply Curve
slides.body:
• Law of Supply: price ↑ → quantity supplied ↑ (ceteris paribus)
• Supply curve slopes upward
• Shift factors: input prices, technology, expectations, number of sellers
• Technology improvement → supply shifts RIGHT (more at each price)
• Input price increase → supply shifts LEFT (less at each price)

slides.title: Market Equilibrium
slides.body:
• Equilibrium: Q_D = Q_S at price P*
• Above P*: surplus (Q_S > Q_D) → price falls
• Below P*: shortage (Q_D > Q_S) → price rises
• Algebraic method: set D equation = S equation, solve for P* and Q*
• Example: Q_D = 100 - 2P, Q_S = 20 + 3P → P* = 16, Q* = 68
slides.speaker_notes: Work through the algebraic example on the board. Then ask: 'What happens if the government sets a price ceiling at P = 10?'

slides.title: Shifts in Equilibrium — Comparative Statics
slides.body:
• Demand ↑ (shift right): P* ↑, Q* ↑
• Supply ↑ (shift right): P* ↓, Q* ↑
• Both shift: direction of one variable is ambiguous
• Real-world example: COVID-19 and hand sanitiser
  Demand ↑ (fear) + Supply ↓ (supply chain) → P definitely ↑, Q ambiguous
slides.speaker_notes: The COVID example is relatable. Use it to teach the 'both shift' case.

prs_hum101_w5_modus.title: HUM101 Week 5 — Modus Ponens and Modus Tollens

slides.title: Argument Forms — Week 5 Overview
slides.body:
Topics:
• Modus ponens (affirming the antecedent)
• Modus tollens (denying the consequent)
• Why these forms are valid
• Common confusion with invalid forms (Week 6 preview)
KC coverage: modus_ponens_structure, deductive_validity_definition
slides.speaker_notes: This week and next week form a pair: valid forms (W5) vs invalid forms that look similar (W6).

slides.title: Modus Ponens — Affirming the Antecedent
slides.body:
Form:
  P1: If P, then Q
  P2: P
  ∴ Q

Example:
  P1: If it rains, the ground is wet
  P2: It is raining
  ∴ The ground is wet

Validity proof: in every row of the truth table where both premises are true, the conclusion is also true.
slides.speaker_notes: Have students verify with a 4-row truth table. Point out that we only check rows where ALL premises are TRUE.

slides.title: Modus Tollens — Denying the Consequent
slides.body:
Form:
  P1: If P, then Q
  P2: Not Q
  ∴ Not P

Example:
  P1: If the battery is dead, the car won't start
  P2: The car started
  ∴ The battery is not dead

Intuition: the conditional creates a chain; denying the end denies the start (contrapositive).
slides.speaker_notes: Students find modus tollens less intuitive than modus ponens. Use the contrapositive equivalence: 'If P then Q' = 'If not Q then not P'.

slides.title: Why These Forms Work — Truth Table Proof
slides.body:
| P | Q | If P then Q | Modus Ponens check | Modus Tollens check |
|T|T| T | P=T, Q=T ✓ | Not applicable (Q true) |
|T|F| F | Premise 1 false | Not applicable |
|F|T| T | P=F, not applicable | Not Q=F, not applicable |
|F|F| T | P=F, not applicable | Not Q=T: conclusion Not P=T ✓ |

Key: no row exists where premises are all true but conclusion is false.

slides.title: Preview: Invalid Look-Alikes (Week 6)
slides.body:
• Affirming the consequent (INVALID):
  If P then Q; Q; therefore P  ✘
  'If it rains the ground is wet; the ground is wet; therefore it rained'
  (Sprinkler could be the cause!)

• Denying the antecedent (INVALID):
  If P then Q; Not P; therefore Not Q  ✘
  'If it rains the ground is wet; it didn't rain; therefore ground isn't wet'
slides.speaker_notes: Ask: 'Can you find a counterexample to each invalid form?' This prepares them for next week's deeper analysis.

slides.title: Matrix Diagonalisation — Week 6 Overview
slides.body:
Topics:
• When is a matrix diagonalisable?
• The diagonalisation procedure: A = PDP⁻¹
• Algebraic vs geometric multiplicity
• Applications: computing A^k efficiently
KC coverage: diagonalisation_conditions, eigenvalue_computation

slides.title: When Can We Diagonalise?
slides.body:
• An n×n matrix A is diagonalisable iff it has n linearly independent eigenvectors
• Sufficient condition: n distinct eigenvalues → always diagonalisable
• Necessary condition: for each eigenvalue λ, geometric multiplicity = algebraic multiplicity
• Geometric multiplicity = dim(null(A - λI))
• Algebraic multiplicity = multiplicity of λ as root of characteristic polynomial
slides.speaker_notes: Common exam question: 'Is this matrix diagonalisable?' Students must check eigenvalue multiplicities.

slides.title: Diagonalisation Procedure
slides.body:
Step 1: Find eigenvalues (solve det(A - λI) = 0)
Step 2: For each λ, find eigenvectors (solve (A - λI)x = 0)
Step 3: Form P = [v₁ | v₂ | ... | vₙ] (eigenvectors as columns)
Step 4: Form D = diag(λ₁, λ₂, ..., λₙ)
Result: A = PDP⁻¹

Verification: AP = PD (each column: Avᵢ = λᵢvᵢ)

slides.title: Example: Diagonalise A = [[4,1],[2,3]]
slides.speaker_notes: Work through this on the board. Then ask students to compute A³ using D.

slides.title: Application: Computing A^k
slides.body:
Since A = PDP⁻¹:
  A² = (PDP⁻¹)(PDP⁻¹) = PD²P⁻¹
  A^k = PD^kP⁻¹
  D^k = diag(λ₁^k, λ₂^k, ..., λₙ^k) ← trivial to compute!

Example: A¹⁰⁰ with A = [[4,1],[2,3]]
  D¹⁰⁰ = [[5¹⁰⁰, 0], [0, 2¹⁰⁰]]
  A¹⁰⁰ = P · D¹⁰⁰ · P⁻¹ (no matrix multiplication 100 times!)
slides.speaker_notes: This is the 'killer app' of diagonalisation. Also mention: Fibonacci sequence via matrix exponentiation.

prs_rsch101_w7_review.title: RSCH101 Week 7 — Midterm Review: Causation and Experimental Design

slides.title: Midterm Review — Week 7 Overview
slides.body:
Review topics:
• Correlation vs causation (Ch. 2-3)
• Confounding variables and threats to internal validity (Ch. 4)
• Experimental vs observational designs (Ch. 5-6)
• Identifying the strongest causal inference from study design
KC coverage: confounding_variable_identification, correlation_does_not_imply_causation
slides.speaker_notes: Format: 30 min review lecture, then 30 min practice problems in groups.

slides.title: Correlation ≠ Causation — Why Not?
slides.body:
• Correlation: two variables move together (Pearson r)
• Three possible explanations for correlation between A and B:
  1. A causes B
  2. B causes A (reverse causation)
  3. C causes both A and B (confounding)
• Classic example: ice cream sales and drowning rates
  Confounder: hot weather causes both
• Correlation tells us NOTHING about which of the 3 is true

slides.title: Confounding Variables
slides.body:
• Confound: a third variable that influences BOTH the IV and DV
• If not controlled, the observed effect may be entirely due to the confound
• Control methods:
  - Random assignment (gold standard: equalises all confounds)
  - Matching (pairs similar participants)
  - Statistical control (regression with confounder as covariate)
• Exam tip: always ask 'Is there a plausible third variable?'

slides.title: Experimental vs Observational Designs
slides.body:
• Experiment: researcher MANIPULATES IV, randomly assigns participants
  → Can infer causation (if well-designed)
• Observational: researcher OBSERVES without manipulation
  → Can only identify associations, not causes
• Quasi-experiment: manipulation without random assignment
  → Stronger than observational, weaker than true experiment
• Key question: 'Did the researcher control who gets the treatment?'
slides.speaker_notes: Give examples of each. Ask students to classify real studies.

slides.title: Practice — Classify These Studies
slides.body:
1. 'Vitamin D supplements reduce flu risk' — participants chose whether to take vitamins
   → Observational (self-selection bias)

2. '100 patients randomly assigned to drug vs placebo'
   → Experiment (random assignment + manipulation)

3. 'Schools in District A got new curriculum, District B kept old'
   → Quasi-experiment (manipulation but no random assignment)

For each: What confounds might exist? Can we infer causation?
slides.speaker_notes: Use think-pair-share. Give 5 min for discussion, then debrief.

prs_phys201_w5_measurement.title: PHYS201 Week 5 — Measurement and Wavefunction Collapse

slides.title: Quantum Measurement — Week 5 Overview
slides.body:
Topics:
• The measurement postulate
• Wavefunction collapse: from superposition to eigenstate
• Born rule: probability = |⟨φ|ψ⟩|²
• Repeated measurements and the Zeno effect (qualitative)
KC coverage: measurement_destroys_coherence, wavefunction_superposition_and_collapse
slides.speaker_notes: This is the most conceptually difficult week. Go slowly and use many visual analogies.

slides.title: The Measurement Postulate
slides.body:
• Before measurement: system in superposition ψ = c₁|φ₁⟩ + c₂|φ₂⟩ + ...
• Measurement of observable A:
  - Result is always an eigenvalue aᵢ of A
  - Probability of getting aᵢ = |cᵢ|² (Born rule)
  - After measurement: state 'collapses' to |φᵢ⟩
• Key: measurement is irreversible and stochastic
• This is fundamentally different from classical physics!
slides.speaker_notes: Use the Stern-Gerlach experiment as a concrete example. Silver atoms: spin up or spin down, nothing in between.

slides.title: Wavefunction Collapse — Visualisation
slides.body:
• Before measurement: probability distribution spread out
  (like a wave across space)
• Measurement: the wave 'collapses' to a spike at the measured value
• Immediately after: system is in eigenstate |φᵢ⟩
• A second identical measurement immediately after gives same result aᵢ (100%)
• But a measurement of a DIFFERENT observable may give uncertain results again
slides.speaker_notes: The 'second measurement gives same result' fact is crucial. It's what distinguishes collapse from noise.

slides.title: Born Rule — Computing Probabilities
slides.body:
Given: ψ = (1/√3)|↑⟩ + √(2/3)|↓⟩

P(spin up) = |1/√3|² = 1/3
P(spin down) = |√(2/3)|² = 2/3
Total: 1/3 + 2/3 = 1 ✓ (normalization)

After measuring spin up:
  New state: |↑⟩ (collapsed)
  P(spin up again) = 1 (certainty)
slides.speaker_notes: Work through normalization check. If |c₁|² + |c₂|² ≠ 1, the state is not physical.

slides.title: Conceptual Questions — Check Your Understanding
slides.body:
Q1: A particle is in state ψ = 0.6|E₁⟩ + 0.8|E₂⟩. What is P(E₁)?
  A: |0.6|² = 0.36

Q2: After measuring E₁, what is the state?
  A: |E₁⟩ (collapsed to eigenstate)

Q3: We immediately measure energy again. What do we get?
  A: E₁ with certainty (state hasn't evolved yet)

Q4: Does measurement 'disturb' the system or 'reveal' pre-existing values?
  A: This is the measurement problem — no consensus! (Bell's theorem: Week 6+)
slides.speaker_notes: Q4 is the philosophical hook. Don't resolve it — just plant the seed for the Copenhagen vs Many-Worlds debate.
